planting.note: Divide or transplant in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to shade; Immortality is a winter-dormant hardy begonia introduced by Plant Delights/JLBG in 2021.

directions: Plant in part shade to shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil; Immortality is a winter-hardy bedding-begonia selection shared by North Carolina gardener Ralph Whisnant in 2014 and introduced by Plant Delights/JLBG in 2021, producing abundant pink flowers through summer on a plant about 2 feet tall. It dies back to the ground each winter and resprouts reliably in spring, without the weedy self-seeding behavior of the straight wax begonia species it derives from. It is a genuine root-hardy perennial for a shaded or part-shade bed, distinct from the Begonia grandis lineage already grown.

planting.note: Plant in spring into sharply drained, humus-rich soil in a sheltered part-shade site; Ginny's outdoor root-hardiness depends heavily on winter drainage, with US sources citing zone 8 but UK sources rating it glasshouse-only — treat as marginal rather than guaranteed hardy.

directions: Plant in a sheltered part-shade site in sharply drained, humus-rich soil; Ginny forms an upright, shrub-like begonia to 2-3 feet with narrow, fuzzy green leaves flushed red beneath, bearing near-continuous soft shell-pink flowers with hot-pink hairs from spring through autumn. Its outdoor hardiness depends heavily on sharp winter drainage rather than being a blanket zone guarantee; US growers report success in zone 8 with dry winter protection, while some UK sources treat it as glasshouse-only. In colder or wetter climates, grow it as a container plant brought under cover for winter.

planting.note: Plant in spring into sharply drained, humus-rich soil in a sheltered part-shade site; Darlene Fuentes shares the same drainage-dependent marginal hardiness as the related cultivar 'Ginny'.

directions: Plant in a sheltered part-shade site in sharply drained, humus-rich soil; Darlene Fuentes shares the same shrubby growth habit and narrow fuzzy leaves as the closely related cultivar 'Ginny,' but bears sprays of small snowy-white flowers instead of pink. Its root-hardiness, like 'Ginny,' depends on sharp winter drainage rather than a guaranteed zone rating, with US growers reporting success around zone 8 with dry winter conditions. In colder or consistently wet-winter climates, grow it as a container plant overwintered under cover.

planting.note: Plant in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Metallic Mist needs a drier winter dormancy rather than consistently wet cold soil.

directions: Plant in part shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil; Metallic Mist is a Terra Nova hybrid with mid-sized palmate leaves densely covered in metallic-silver variegation, giving the rex-begonia look of a houseplant on a genuinely root-hardy outdoor plant. It is reported hardy to USDA zone 7, possibly zone 6 with excellent drainage, but needs a dry-ish winter dormancy rather than consistently wet, cold soil to survive. Its foliage color makes it a strong textural accent among the plainer-leaved hardy begonia cultivars already in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant in spring into sharply drained, humus-rich soil in part shade; Connee Boswell is grown chiefly for its metallic pink-toned foliage.

directions: Plant in part shade in sharply drained, humus-rich soil; Connee Boswell bears palmate foliage with a distinctive metallic pink tone on a shrubby begonia grown primarily for its foliage color rather than flowers. It is reported root-hardy to around USDA zone 8, or perhaps colder, when given sharp drainage over winter. It is a modestly available named cultivar found through specialty begonia and tropical-plant retailers rather than general garden centers.

planting.note: Plant in spring into sharply drained, humus-rich soil in part shade; Begonia parilis is grown for its toughness and outdoor survival rather than showy flowers or foliage.

directions: Plant in part shade in sharply drained, humus-rich soil; Begonia parilis is a shrub-like, thick-stemmed species with unassuming foliage, noted in horticultural literature as a long-neglected but genuinely tenacious garden survivor rather than a showy ornamental. It is reported root-hardy to roughly USDA zone 8, perhaps lower with winter protection. It is the least showy of the hardy outdoor begonias but the most botanically distinct addition, valued by collectors for its demonstrated toughness in marginal outdoor conditions.
